label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.quote: The conductor's first scheduled wake with a record made deck's programme of experiments the team's queue.
findings.why: As a newcomer I do not know what a wake, a scheduled wake or a record is yet, and the sentence stacks all three with names I have not met.

findings.quote: gone out with its first push. The researcher redacted it in the files
findings.why: Push and redacted are programmer words used with no gloss, and this is the first failure I am meant to care about.

findings.quote: That is the lesson the register draws: redaction does not reach a commit already pushed.
findings.why: Register, redaction and commit are all unexplained, so the lesson lands as jargon for someone who has only used an app builder.

findings.quote: It is the first sign in the record of members pacing each other
findings.why: The narrator reports from the record with no I and no hindsight, where the editor could say what he made of it.

findings.quote: The argument is in the wake record, both halves of it
findings.why: The scene has just been played out line by line and this sentence tells it again as a summary.

findings.quote: the factory as a value chain: what I wanted at the top
findings.why: The map is described before the Wardley map is explained two lines later, and value chain is a word I have to guess.
The five steps are mentioned as if known, yet a reader of this chapter alone has not been told what they are.

findings.quote: opened and never closed on the team's branch
findings.why: Session, branch and closed are programmer talk with no gloss, and it is the sort of line that makes this feel written for coders.

findings.quote: The record shows exactly that: the refusal, and the question sent to me in its place.
findings.why: Studio's line just above has already told the refusal and the question, so this tells the scene twice.

findings.quote: Part one was final and not yet locked. The lock tool existed. One session was open
findings.why: Three short sentences in a row, each leaning on terms (locked, session) I only half understood.

findings.quote: You do not need my nine. You need one.
findings.why: Nine of what is never said on this page, so the best line for a beginner starts with a small stall.

findings.quote: the ones Start here gave you as a formula
findings.why: It assumes I read an earlier page and remember its formula; as a first-build finisher dropping in here I did not.
The Rests on and The moment lines are full of commits, briefs and chapter references, which is the moment I feel this is for programmers.

findings.quote: Share the brief, the board and the hold, and each of you runs your own agents.
findings.why: Board and hold are team vocabulary I have not been given a plain meaning for, and the step is otherwise easy to take.

findings.quote: That is the whole method. A brief and rules in plain words. A check every change passes.
findings.why: A chain of short sentences and a list in a row; it sounds like a slogan rather than the editor thinking aloud.

what_holds: 08-hours-four-and-five-before-dawn.md: the two failures kept in, with Dev's 'The branch wins.' and the researcher owning its late review, are characters I can follow.
15-hour-eighteen-faster-than-the-clock.md: 'the brakes are what let you go fast' and Studio asking the editor instead of trusting a relayed word are the clearest ideas so far.
23-principles-and-build-your-own.md: the shop owner and newsroom examples, 'An app builder works too', and the stop-line check are a step I could take tomorrow.
notes: Chapters 8 and 15 read as a log of a team I have not met; chapter 23 is where I could start. The Rests on lines are the part most likely to make a non-programmer feel the book is not for them. None.
